extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, and readers interested in research integrity and academic publishing (especially mathematics)
extracted.subtask_description: Identification and description of causes, flags, and editorial responses that lead to retractions or expressions of concern in mathematics research publications. Focuses on problems with peer review, authorship, data, proofs, duplication, and plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiently rigorous peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer-review process was “less rigorous than the journal requires.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retractions or withdrawals can follow when journals determine the review process did not meet their standards; example: a special issue whose review process was judged inadequate leading to its retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest in editorial/peer-review role
rubrics_metrics.description: A guest editor coordinated the peer-review process while also being an author on the majority of papers in the issue (author on 11 of the 13 papers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals view this as a major conflict of interest; official retraction notes can focus on conflict-of-interest concerns and may prompt re-review or withdrawal of a whole issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-coordinated / self peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: An author or guest editor oversees or coordinates reviews for papers they authored (self peer review / author’s coordination of peer review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice is flagged as unacceptable; journals may issue an expression of concern and arrange independent re-review by reviewers not chosen by the author in question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest errors (incorrect proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: An incorrect proof or honest mathematical error that undermines the paper’s main result (e.g., 'an incorrect proof has felled a math paper').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such genuine mistakes (not malpractice) can lead authors to retract papers; retraction notes commonly state the issue as an honest error rather than malfeasance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gap in the proof / false application of a theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'gap in the proof' resulting from a 'false application' of a theorem or similar logical mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When critical reasoning steps are invalid, authors or editors may retract the paper; retraction notices often describe the specific logical failings, e.g., false application of a theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erroneous or significantly flawed data
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers containing 'significant errors in the data' that materially affect results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data errors can lead quickly to retraction, especially when they invalidate findings or analyses; examples include simulation papers retracted soon after publication due to flawed data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dispute over authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorship disputes noted in the retraction context (e.g., disagreement about who should be credited as authors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflicts over authorship, sometimes appearing alongside data errors, can contribute to editorial decisions to retract papers or issue notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicate publication / identical papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication of an 'identical' version of a paper in another journal (duplicate publication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals retract papers when an identical or substantially overlapping version is published elsewhere; retraction notes cite duplication as the reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Detection of plagiarism in a paper (text or results copied from prior work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plagiarism cases frequently result in retraction; examples include older papers retracted years later after plagiarism was detected and documented in retraction notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of concern leading to re-review
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals issuing an 'expression of concern' and deciding to re-review affected articles (often after discovering procedural problems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An expression of concern is an interim editorial action that signals possible problems (e.g., inappropriate handling of peer review); subsequent independent re-review may follow and result in retraction or correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological problems / unreliable findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological flaws or problems that render findings unreliable (listed as 'methodological problems' / 'unreliable findings').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When methods are fundamentally flawed or results cannot be trusted, editors may retract or correct the literature to prevent propagation of false conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial remedy: withdrawal or conversion to another format
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors or editors withdraw issues or papers (e.g., author withdrew an entire issue saying it would be better suited as a book).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withdrawal can be voluntary (author-initiated) or editorial; in some cases, withdrawal is used as a remedy when publication format or process is deemed inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taggable categories as retraction reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Common categorical labels used to classify problematic papers on the site: e.g., 'self peer review', 'duplication retractions', 'plagiarism', 'authorship issues', 'data issues', 'methodological problems', 'unreliable findings'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These tags summarize recurrent themes and help readers and editors recognize patterns of misconduct or error across cases; they indicate the taxonomy of causes that lead to editorial actions.
